claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has severe local lattice distortions.
Chemical complexity in equimolar WTaTiVZr modifies its dislocation cores.
The modified dislocation cores reduce conventional dislocation pinning relative to pure tungsten.
Reduced pinning in WTaTiVZr promotes dislocation cross-slip during high-temperature deformation.
The lattice distortion and chemical complexity of WTaTiVZr promote grain-boundary sliding during high-temperature deformation.
Cross-slip and grain-boundary sliding provide dynamic recovery in WTaTiVZr.
Dynamic recovery gives WTaTiVZr greater high-temperature plastic strain than commercially pure tungsten.
Dynamic recovery gives WTaTiVZr greater high-temperature toughness than commercially pure tungsten.
Cross-slip and grain-boundary sliding are minimal in pure tungsten under the stated high-temperature conditions.
High-temperature constant-strain-rate tensile testing from 1000°C to 1500°C under identical high-vacuum conditions is the proposed controlled comparison.
The HEA and pure-tungsten specimens are to be fully dense, homogeneous, recrystallized, and matched in grain size.
Controlling grain size and phase stability is intended to isolate the effects of lattice distortion and chemical complexity.
Mechanical loading at 1000°C to 1500°C in high vacuum is relevant to sustained plasma-facing-component service.
Relative to pure tungsten, WTaTiVZr is predicted to show more cross-slip and dislocation-annihilation events.
Relative to pure tungsten, WTaTiVZr is predicted to show greater grain-boundary-sliding activity.
The hypothesis is limited to homogeneous, phase-stable microstructures tested at approximately 1000°C to 1500°C.
Failure to observe both enhanced mechanical performance and the proposed dislocation or grain-boundary activity, after microstructural controls, would falsify the hypothesis.
